messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Kwame, a 68‑year‑old African American policy analyst, first went to the emergency department in late summer, he thought it was another routine checkup. Instead, the pounding in his chest was unmistakable. An ECG revealed a blocked coronary artery, and a cardiologist told him the blockage had already caused a small infarction. By midnight he had a diagnosis that shook his sense of life: he was no longer immune to death. That night, the image of the white‑collared doctor holding his trembling hand became a permanent imprint in his mind. From that point, Kwame’s view of his own body turned hostile. He began to think, “I will never feel normal emotions again,” and “my body keeps reacting as if danger is still looming.” These negative appraisals made him perceive the world through a lens of constant threat. He could no longer trust his own sensations; even a quiet cough or the rumble of the refrigerator triggered a wave of anxiety, as if a second attack might be imminent. The belief that his body was unreliable amplified his sense that danger could arise at any moment, heightening his hypervigilance throughout his days. The memory of the ER scene was not a quiet recollection; it burst into his consciousness whenever he heard a sudden noise. A ringing phone in the policy office, a siren outside the building, or even the hum of the office air‑conditioning would pull him back to that night of terror. In those moments, the past and present collapsed into a single, overpowering instant, and he felt his heart pounding in his chest as if he were again in the ER. The intensity of the memory was so great that when it returned, he would stop mid‑sentence, breathing hard, feeling the weight of his fear pressing down on him. Kwame’s persistent state of threat fed back into these intrusive memories. While he sat at his desk, surrounded by reports and deadlines, his mind kept drifting to that night. The feeling of imminent danger, even in a safe environment, made it impossible for him to stay focused. He would glance at the clock, feel a sudden surge of tension, and then be drawn back to the memory that felt more real than the spreadsheet before him. The cycle of threat and memory kept tightening, each intrusion reinforcing the other, and the office became a silent arena where his panic played out repeatedly. Threat also reinforced Kwame’s negative appraisals. Each time the threat sense surged—when a patient’s report came in or a supervisor called—he reminded himself that his body was a weapon against which he could not defend. The belief that he could no longer feel normal emotions solidified, and his trust in his own body eroded further. He began to think that any small discomfort could be a sign of impending catastrophe, and the resulting dread made the notion of “normal” feel distant and unattainable. In practice, the loop took a concrete toll. Concentration faltered; he found himself making errors in policy briefs that had previously been routine. When a client asked him a question, he could only respond after a few frantic breaths, feeling that each answer might trigger another spike in his threat state. His colleagues noticed the changes, but he would explain that he was simply tired. At home, he kept his phone off his bedside table because the buzz of incoming calls would jolt him back into that night. He no longer walked down the hallway to the bathroom; instead, he stayed in his bedroom, feeling the walls close in, as if the ER’s sterile lights were never far away. The isolation deepened his grief over his late wife, making him retreat further from the small support circle he had once cherished. The decision to seek help came after Kwame realized that each day he could no longer perform his job without the constant anxiety that gnawed at him. One evening, while staring at a spreadsheet that should have been simple, he felt his chest tighten so severely that he nearly fainted. He could not shake the sense that a second attack was looming, even though the building’s lights were dim and the office empty. In that moment of panic, he understood that he had reached a point where the threat of the memory was more destructive than the illness that had initially triggered it. He reached for therapy, hoping to untangle the web of threat, memory, and negative appraisal that had tightened around his life, and to regain even a sliver of trust in his own body.
